newsitem.title: CANADA: NYMEX hopes to refuel Alberta gas futures interest.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX hopes to refuel Alberta gas futures interest.

text.p: The New York Mercantile Exchange plans to mount a promotional campaign and possibly offer incentives aimed at boosting trading interest in its unpopular Alberta natural gas futures contract, a NYMEX offical said on Monday.

"We try as much as possible to have a presence at the large market functions and you can expect a greater NYMEX presence in the coming months as we look to get things up and going with this contract," Daniel McElduff, the exchange's manager of energy research, told Reuters following a speech to a gas conference.
"Hopefully we'll have something beyond the norm to offer to the marketplace to help to promote that."

McElduff said NYMEX had yet to determine what incentives it might use to bolster trading volume in the Alberta contract, launched last September as a regional alternative to the successful contract for gas delivered at Henry Hub, Louisiana.
The Alberta contract, for gas delivered at various points along the NOVA Corp pipeline system, was launched with some fanfare and trading volume was brisk at first.
However, most of the 29 billion cubic feet of gas traded under the the Alberta contract was moved in its first few days.

McElduff said a combination of factors -- some related to events in Canada's gas industry -- led to a lack of liquidity in the new contract, which was launched at the same time as southwest U.S. Permian Basin gas futures.
Many potential players were already in the midst of forging long-term contract and hedging deals related to Canada's November-October gas year when the futures were launched, he said.
Also, gas market volatility last autumn, which resulted in bankruptcies among several small Canadian marketers, kept attention focused away from learning and trading a new contract, he said.
The lack of activity among producers and end-users left little opportunity for professional speculators to move into the market, McElduff said.
"Someone really needs to perform the market-maker function and it's something that's usually provided by our floor -- our local community," he said.

"Right now, there's not a great deal of incentive for them to come into the Alberta ring because of the opportunities they have in other markets. Until they see a steady stream of commercial participation, they're going to be reluctant."

Like the Henry Hub futures, the Alberta contract size is 10,000 million British thermal units and is priced in U.S. dollars per mmBtu. One reason for its launch was to reduce risks associated with the different regional markets.
McElduff said there were no plans to cancel the contract, citing the example of sour crude oil and Gulf Coast unleaded gasoline contracts, which are still listed but not traded.
